text-align: center;\"\u003E5•WHAT IS THE REASON FOR HIS COMA??\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"separator\" style=\"clear: both; text-align: center;\"\u003E\u003Ca href=\"https:\/\/www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov\/pmc\/articles\/PMC4606267\/\"\u003Ehttps:\/\/www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov\/pmc\/articles\/PMC4606267\/\u003C\/a\u003E\u003Cbr \/\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"separator\" style=\"clear: both; text-align: center;\"\u003E\u003Cbr \/\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"separator\" style=\"clear: both; text-align: center;\"\u003ETuberculous meningitis (TBM) is still a crippling disease with a high degree of morbidity and mortality. One of the most severe complications of TBM is stroke resulting from vascular involvement. In HIV-infected individuals with TBM, the immune response to the tuberculous bacilli is altered; therefore, pathological features are very different from those seen in patients with relatively normal cell-mediated immunity (CMI). The brains of such individuals showed minimal inflammatory response with parenchymal infarcts and vasculitis, not only in the basal ganglia but in the cortical parenchyma as well.\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"separator\" style=\"clear: both; text-align: center;\"\u003E\u003Cbr \/\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"separator\" style=\"clear: both; text-align: center;\"\u003E\u003Cbr \/\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"separator\" style=\"clear: both; text-align: center;\"\u003E\u003Ca href=\"https:\/\/www.cambridge.org\/core\/books\/uncommon-causes-of-stroke\/vasculitis-and-stroke-due-to-tuberculosis\/ACB91EF45660A1B7AAD98C17E3DE2701\"\u003Ehttps:\/\/www.cambridge.org\/core\/books\/uncommon-causes-of-stroke\/vasculitis-and-stroke-due-to-tuberculosis\/ACB91EF45660A1B7AAD98C17E3DE2701\u003C\/a\u003E\u003Cbr \/\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"separator\" style=\"clear: both; text-align: center;\"\u003E\u003Cbr \/\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"separator\" style=\"clear: both; text-align: center;\"\u003E\u003Cbr \/\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"separator\" style=\"clear: both; text-align: center;\"\u003E6•WHAT IS THE REASON FOR HIGH SUGAR AND LOW PROTEIN IN CSF IN MENINGITIS??\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"separator\" style=\"clear: both; text-align: center;\"\u003EDuring bacterial infection, the protein level in the CSF goes up, due to the\u0026nbsp;increased numbers of replicating bacteria and body cells fighting the infection, with both of them having a high concentration of protein. High levels of lactate in CSF indicate a higher likelihood of bacterial meningitis.\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"separator\" style=\"clear: both; text-align: center;\"\u003E\u003Cbr \/\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"separator\" style=\"clear: both; text-align: center;\"\u003EPeople with bacterial meningitis typically have low levels of CSF glucose because of\u0026nbsp;glycolysis by both white cells and the pathogen and impaired CSF glucose transport. The level of CSF glucose is typically interpreted in relation to that of serum glucose, since glucose passes across the blood–brain barrier.\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"separator\" style=\"clear: both;
